title: Soil geography

definition.text: The branch of physical geography that deals with how soils are distributed across the terrain.

facts.text: It studies the spatial distribution of soils in relation to topography, climate, soil life and the minerals within soils.
It sits beside geomorphology, climatology, hydrology and biogeography among the fields that study the Earth's surface.
Understanding pedogenesis explains soil distribution patterns today, the concern of soil geography, and in past geologic periods, the concern of paleopedology.
Pedodiversity was brought into pedology to analyse soil spatial patterns and soil geography and to test theories of soil formation.
The Russian Geographical Society awarded Konstantin Glinka its Lütke Gold Medal for his work on soil geography.

notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own; mentioned on Physical geography, Natural science, Soil formation, Pedodiversity and Konstantin Glinka.

title: Tropical soils

definition.text: The soils of the humid tropics, most of them strongly leached and poor in nutrients, though some areas are fertile.

facts.text: On younger substrates, especially volcanic ones, tropical soils can be quite fertile.
Most cation exchange capacity sits on clay and humus colloids; fast leaching and decomposition in hot, wet climates remove them, explaining the apparent infertility of tropical soils.
Phosphorus is often the most deficient nutrient, because intense leaching and weathering deplete the mineral pool and, unlike nitrogen, it cannot be replenished from the air.
Leaching removes silica and leaves iron and aluminium sesquioxides, giving many tropical soils their characteristic red colour.
Unlike loess, tropical soils draw their fertility almost wholly from organic matter, whose humus holds nutrient ions and releases them to roots.
Stripped of vegetation, for example by deforestation, they can develop a surface hardpan of laterite or bauxite, a known case of irreversible degradation.
Abundant deep burrowers such as ants, termites and worms mean tropical soils often lack the argillic Bt horizons of midlatitude soils, and stonelayers often mark the base of the biomantle.
Charcoal, or biochar, is used to improve nutrient-poor tropical soils, an approach modelled on the fertile Amazonian terra preta.

notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own; passes test 5 (used on many in-scope pages).

title: Lithosequence

definition.text: A set of soils formed under similar conditions on different parent materials, so that their profiles differ because of the parent material.

facts.text: Because the soils share similar weathering conditions, differences in composition reflect the relative weathering rates of the parent minerals.
The Goldich dissolution series, which ranks minerals by weathering rate, can be applied to lithosequences.
Studies of lithosequences give the clearest picture of the role of parent material in soil formation, including in paleosols.

notes: Phrase concept 'Climosequence, lithosequence and biosequence': only lithosequence has sentences; climosequence and biosequence have none. Mentioned on Goldich dissolution series and Paleopedology.

title: Soils of Australia

definition.text: The soils of the Australian continent, many of them extremely ancient and naturally deficient in phosphorus.

facts.text: Plants with proteoid (cluster) roots can grow in these very nutrient-poor soils, and their dense root-hair networks can absorb enough rain to prevent runoff.
The Australian Soil Classification replaced earlier systems for Australian soils, including the Factual Key (1960) and the Handbook of Australian Soils (1968).
James Arthur Prescott described them in CSIR bulletin 52, The Soils of Australia in Relation to Vegetation and Climate.

notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own; mentioned on Cluster root, Surface runoff, Australian Soil Classification, Handbook of Australian Soils and James Arthur Prescott. Regional, but named by the syllabus.

title: Soils of British Columbia and Yukon

definition.text: British Columbia and Yukon have the greatest diversity of soils in Canada, from a varied geologic history, rugged mountain and valley terrain and wide climate range.

facts.text: The region holds all ten soil orders of the Canadian system, reflecting the full range of soil-forming factors.

Podzols have the largest extent in British Columbia, on acidic parent materials under cool, humid conditions; Luvisols are the other dominant order, on loamy glacial tills in the Interior plateaus and boreal forest.

Cryosols occur in permafrost areas of northern Yukon and on high mountain peaks; Chernozems occur only in the arid Central Interior, with Brown, Dark Brown and Black types as the climate turns more humid northward.

Regosols occur on landslide-prone and avalanche-prone slopes and the Fraser Delta; Gleysols are common in low-lying coastal areas, and artificially drained ones in the Fraser Valley are among the province's most productive farm soils.
Mining here leaves Anthroposols; in metal mining the main concern is acid rock drainage, because sulphide minerals such as pyrite weather rapidly to sulfuric acid.

title: Soils of the Prairie Provinces

definition.text: The soils of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba are the most heavily converted to farmland in Canada, with the soil pattern set by bedrock geology and the rain shadow of the Western Cordillera.

facts.text: In the south over 80% of the land is agricultural, and the type of farming follows soil capability; true prairie covers only the southern part of these provinces.

About one-third of the region sits on igneous and metamorphic Canadian Shield rock and two-thirds on sedimentary rock; igneous rock yields acidic sandy, gravelly parent materials, sedimentary rock neutral to alkaline loamy ones.
Chernozems dominate the southern grassland, Luvisols the northern mixed forest, Brunisols the acidic Shield, and Organic Cryosols the cold, saturated peats near Hudson Bay.
Crops once centred on spring wheat with summerfallow; today canola, pulses and flax are grown and most producers use continuous cultivation with conservation tillage or no-till.
Under the Canada Land Inventory, classes 1 to 4 sustain field crops and classes 5 and 6 suit only forage; texture decides class mainly through its effect on water availability.

related: Soils of British Columbia and Yukon

definition.text: Chernozemic great groups across the Prairies follow the zonation of native grasses, which in turn follows the regional water deficit.

facts.text: Great groups of the Chernozemic order are separated by the colour of the A horizon, which shows how much organic carbon the grasses added.
In the driest part, with an annual water deficit near 200 mm, low grasses with little biomass give Brown Chernozems; less deficit to the west and north gives Dark Brown and Black Chernozems.
Organic carbon is highest in southern Manitoba, where the annual water deficit is only about 70 mm.
Chernozems have organically enriched Ah horizons over decalcified, slightly reddened Bm horizons.

definition.text: Moving north from the grassland, soils change through the transitional Parkland zone to continuous Mixedwood forest, as tree litter replaces grass as the main organic input.

facts.text: In the Parkland the Ah horizon lightens and begins to bleach, forming an Ahe horizon; these are Dark Gray Chernozems.
Further north an LFH litter layer sits on the mineral soil over a bleached Ae horizon and a clay-richer Bt horizon, which is underlain by a carbonate-bearing C horizon; these are Gray Luvisols.
Gray Luvisols also form on glacio-lacustrine deposits in north-central Manitoba.

definition.text: Ontario soils formed mostly in parent materials left by the Wisconsinan Laurentide Ice Sheet, and their distribution follows three ecozones with different dominant soil-forming factors.

facts.text: The ice retreated northeast, exposing southern Ontario as much as 13,000 years ago and the far north about 8,500 to 6,500 years ago.

In the Hudson Plains ecozone (about 25% of Ontario) cold, semi-arid climate dominates: low evapotranspiration plus water-retentive clayey and silty glacio-marine materials leave much moisture in the soil, over neutral to alkaline limestones.

The Boreal Shield (about 66%) lies on acidic, weathering-resistant Precambrian gneiss and granite, and its soils vary with climate, parent material, topography and vegetation; Dystric Brunisols dominate the west.

The Mixedwood Plains (about 9%) rest on carbonate-rich limestones, so soils depend mainly on parent material, with climate less important; it holds Ontario's most productive farmland and its major cities.
The Guelph series, a Brunisolic Gray-Brown Luvisol formed in loam to silt loam moraine, became Ontario's provincial soil in 2015 and is prime agricultural soil when not limited by slope.

definition.text: Quebec has seven soil orders arranged in a zonal pattern from south to north, set by climate, vegetation, time since glaciation and parent material.

facts.text: Soils formed over the last 6,000 to 10,000 years after the Laurentide Ice Sheet retreated, on parent materials that follow the geology of the Canadian Shield, the Appalachians and the sedimentary St. Lawrence valley.
After glaciation the Champlain Sea left salt-rich clay in the St. Lawrence Lowlands; leaching of the salt and river incision made these clays unstable, causing over 700 landslides and earthflows.

Podzols cover 39% of Quebec, mostly Humo-Ferric great groups on the Boreal and Taiga Shield; Brunisols cover 17%, mostly Dystric, where profile development is too weak for Podzols; Organic soils cover 8%, mainly Mesisols.
Dystric Brunisols can turn into Podzols over several thousand years, as in sandy deposits exposed by sea-level fall on the North Shore, where sesquioxide-cemented Bfc horizons replace the Bm horizon.

Only a small area has high agricultural potential: Canada Land Inventory Classes 1 to 3 total about 0.28 ha per Quebecer, the smallest of any province, and about 80% of them are cropland, so conserving them matters.

title: Phosphorus as a marker of past human occupation

facts.text: Ancient hearths changed soil morphology in northern Quebec, and disposal of fish and caribou bones raised soil phosphorus above undisturbed levels, especially the calcium phosphate fraction.
Acid soils there preserve bones poorly, so archaeological evidence for people there over 3000 years ago is hard to find.

definition.text: Seven of Canada's ten soil orders occur in Atlantic Canada, but heavy precipitation and coarse, acidic glacial till make Podzols the dominant soil.

facts.text: Soils are often stony or shallow to bedrock, so the four provinces hold only about 1.5% of Canada's farmland, and only Prince Edward Island has more farmland than forest.

The region has four ecozones: Atlantic Maritime (New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island), Boreal Shield (Newfoundland), Taiga Shield (most of Labrador) and Arctic Cordillera in the far north.

The Atlantic Maritime is warmest, about 7 degrees C with 1250 mm of rain a year, on mostly sedimentary Paleozoic rock; Taiga Shield and Arctic Cordillera are colder, on Precambrian gneiss and granite with thin till and exposed rock.
Surficial geology is mostly glacial till of variable thickness, with locally important glacio-fluvial deposits.

By the Canada Land Inventory the region has no Class 1 land; Class 2 is about 588,000 ha, Class 3 about 2,275,000 ha and Class 4 about 2,507,000 ha, and most of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland is Class 7.

title: Soil influence on forest composition in Atlantic Canada

facts.text: In the Atlantic Maritime ecozone soils influence tree species and productivity more than in the Boreal and Taiga Shield, where climate is the main driver.

Sandy or very gravelly Humo-Ferric Podzols, sometimes cemented, favour black spruce and pines adapted to dry, poor soils, while loamy, fertile soils with more Ferro-Humic Podzols support a wider tree mix.
Shallow or stony soils limit productivity and raise windthrow hazard, and windthrow in deeper soils mixes horizons and creates buried horizons.

definition.text: Dykeland soils are farmland made from reclaimed tidal salt marsh behind dykes, as built in Atlantic Canada by Acadian settlers in the 1700s.

facts.text: Dykes, land forming, a drainage network and hand-made aboiteaux (sluice gates) created over 33,000 ha of farmland.
The dominant Acadia series is a Regosol: flat silt loam to silty clay loam, imperfectly drained, with little horizon development and periodic flooding.
These fertile soils have long grown forage and more recently silage corn and soybeans; Grand Pre in Nova Scotia, over 1300 ha, became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2012.
